Economy & Markets
• Alphabet and Tesla flagged soaring AI capex that is weighing on margins and testing investor patience despite revenue growth.

Economy & Markets.title: Burnham offers 20% cut in business rates for pubs, clubs and live music in England – UK politics live
Economy & Markets.text: The prime minister said the £100m package would mean the typical pub would save around £1,100 in the next financial yearGood morning and welcome to the UK politics live blog.Andy Burnham will cut business rate bills for pubs, clubs and live music venues in England by 20% from next April.For too long, governments have stood by while cherished venues have disappeared from our local high streets. So today I am changing that.This government will back the businesses that people want to see in their communities. I said I would protect pubs and local high streets – the beating heart of our communities – and that’s what we will do.The new chancellor, John Healey, said the government would return to its commitment to overhaul the wider business rates system, including small business rates relief, at the budget.Ministers also plan to crack down on businesses that sell through online marketplaces but do not comply with their tax obligations, putting them at an unfair advantage over those that do, and is consulting on measures to make those marketplaces more responsible for this.Burnham announced that the government would cut VAT on electricity bills, reducing them by an average of £45 a year from October. This would be funded, officials said, by his decision to scrap the digital ID scheme.The prime minister also announced he would reduce the fare cap from £3 a journey to £2 next year, funded mainly by changing international climate donations into repayable loans.Burnham is immersed in a deepening political row after ordering a review of plans for the early release of thousands of killers, rapists and sex offenders from prison in September.Victims of crime have accused ministers of making “cheap jokes” about releasing prisoners early after Wes Streeting and Shabana Mahmood were caught on camera “ribbing” about the scheme.Scottish Labour’s rivals in Holyrood have slammed Anas Sarwar’s shock decision to resign as leader to sit in Andy Burnham’s new government, calling him a “chancer” and accusing him of lying to voters.The Conservatives have asked HMRC to investigate whether Nigel Farage should have paid tax on the £5m gift he received from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. Science & Technology.title: The Computer That Helped Win World War II
Science & Technology.text: One summer day in 1941, a British radio operator was monitoring German military frequencies and heard something unexpected in her headphones. A later report called it “strange new music.” Sounding unlike the familiar Morse dit-dit-dah of enciphered messages sent over the German Enigma network, the “new music” was a rhythmic warble of binary teletype code being transmitted at high speed.Germany’s wartime engineers had developed a radically new encryption and transmission system. It was way more advanced than Enigma, which was patented in 1920.To break the complex new cipher, engineer Tommy Flowers built Colossus, the world’s first large-scale programmable electronic digital computer. Flowers previously built Enigma-related codebreaking equipment for Alan Turing, the British mathematician.Colossus was installed in the British codebreaking headquarters at Bletchley Park, about 80 kilometers from London. The room-size machine weighed around a tonne.The computer is being commemorated as an IEEE Milestone. The dedication ceremony is scheduled to be held 29 September at Bletchley Park.Decrypting Germany’s strange new musicBritain’s top codebreakers were quickly all over the new “music” being picked up by the intercept stations. Identifying it as encrypted teletype code was the easy part. The real problem was figuring out how the encryption machine worked. Its manufacturer was discovered at the end of the war: Berlin engineering firm C. Lorenz.But in 1941, the Lorenz machine was just a black box to the British. They codenamed it “Tunny,” a British term for tuna fish. The Enigma breakers had set a precedent for using piscine codenames such as Dolphin, Lumpsucker, and Porpoise.Enigma had three or four encrypting wheels. The codebreakers guessed that the Tunny machine also used a system of rotating wheels to encrypt messages. An important clue was that all the intercepted messages shared a curious feature: Each began with an uncoded list of 12 common German names, including Anton, Bertha, Conrad, and Dora. The codebreakers guessed that Tunny had 12 wheels and that the 12 names and their order somehow told the receiving operator which combination they should twist the wheels to before decrypting the message.Then the British had an extraordinary piece of good fortune. John Tiltman, head of the research section at Bletchley Park, started analyzing a pair of intercepted messages, each around 1,200 characters long. Unusually, both began with the same sequence of names. The second message turned out to be a retype of the first, with minor differences in punctuation, a few abbreviations, and other small divergences. Tiltman managed to decrypt the two ciphertexts using a mixture of educated guesswork and intuition. The resulting 1,200 or so pairings of ciphertext and plaintext characters proved to be enough information to deduce the workings of the Tunny machine.That was thanks to Bill Tutte, a quiet young codebreaker who spent weeks poring over the pairings. One day, he shyly announced to his superiors how Tunny worked. His description was uncannily accurate.The next step in the Tunny machine’s downfall was achieved by Turing, fresh from his successes against Enigma.Knowledge of how the Tunny machine worked was not enough to decrypt the messages. Codebreakers also required detailed information about how the wheels of the sender’s machine had been set up. There were adjustable pins around the circumference of each wheel: In one of its two possible positions, a pin would contribute a 1 to the encryption process, and in the other, a 0. The pins were reset from time to time.The codebreakers also needed to know the wheels’ positions at the start of the message—which the German operators gave away in the list of 12 names.Turing invented a tricky method, called “Turingery,” that enabled codebreakers to deduce the positions of the pins from nothing but intercepted ciphertext.After that, the message could be decrypted, using the list of names and a British replica of the Tunny machine.The basis of Turingery was a procedure that Turing introduced, called “delta-ing” (from the Greek letter delta). Also known as “differencing,” the process used “sideways” addition: To delta the four letters ABCD, you add (at the bit level) A to B, B to C, and C to D. Turing used delta-ing to reveal information about the wheels.Tunny messages, often signed by Adolph Hitler himself, turned out to be pure gold for the Allies. The machine was used in Berlin by the Armed Forces High Command to communicate with front-line generals directing the war in the Eastern and Western theaters.Once the system was broken, the Allies could eavesdrop on lengthy back-and-forth communications between the architects of Germany’s battle plans.Turingery was the codebreakers’ only weapon against Tunny for a year, during which they managed to decrypt 1.5 million letters of ciphertext.But everything changed when those helpful lists of names at the start of each message disappeared.At the same time, Turingery was becoming less effective. Turing’s method depended on the German sender mistakenly using the same wheel settings to encrypt two differing messages. As security tightened across the Tunny network, the blunder became rarer.Fortunately, Tutte had been at work devising a different decryption method, based on Turing’s delta-ing but taking a novel approach.Building the Colossus computerTutte had found a way of deducing wheel information from ciphertext, with no list of names or blunders by the German operators required. His method made use of statistical properties of the Tunny machine itself.At first, it wasn’t clear how to apply his statistical method, however. The Tunny breakers worked by hand. Applying Turingery to a message was like solving a monster Sudoku or crossword puzzle.Tutte’s statistical method required scads of routine binary math, as well as a colossal amount of counting long binary sequences. If the process were done by hand, one message could take months to decrypt. What was needed was a machine to automate the process. Engineer Thomas H. Flowers developed Colossus to break a complexnew German cipher.Pictorial Press/AlamyThe first plan was to build a machine from electromagnetic relays, adding a couple of dozen vacuum tubes to speed up the counting. Electronic tubes were much faster than electromagnetic relays, which had slow-moving metal components. Problems with the circuit design bedeviled the machine’s relay-based logic unit, however.Flowers was recommended by Turing and brought in to troubleshoot. He was on loan to Bletchley Park from the Post Office Research Station in London, where he had spent the prewar years designing experimental switching equipment involving thousands of vacuum tubes.At the time, it was commonly believed that tubes could not be used in large numbers because each one contained a hot filament. This meant tubes were prone to sudden death. In a large installation, it would not be long before one tube blew and things stopped working properly.Flowers discovered that switching tubes on and off stressed them, but leaving them on continuously made them more reliable than relays. He offered to build Bletchley Park a high-speed, all-electronic machine containing around 2,000 tubes.Bletchley Park’s advisors rejected the idea, convinced that such a machine would never work reliably. But Flowers, confident of his proposed design, retreated to his London laboratory and quietly built the electronic machine that he believed the codebreakers needed. He and his small team of engineers worked day and night for 10 months to create Colossus.In January 1944 some of his engineers showed up at Bletchley Park with the world’s first large-scale programmable electronic digital computer packed onto the back of a truck. Colossus was reassembled and functional in about two weeks, and it notched up its first German message on 5 February 1944.The machine read the input—Tunny ciphertext—photoelectrically from a large loop of punched paper tape. The output—information about the wheels—went to a primitive printer that Flowers’ engineers had created from a manual typewriter, fitting relays to automate the keys. Once Colossus had cracked enough of the Tunny machine’s wheels, the information was passed on to the hand-breakers, who took over.The codebreakers were astonished by Colossus.“I don’t think they understood very clearly what I was proposing until they actually had the machine,” Flowers said in a 1977 interview. “They just couldn’t believe it!”Colossus was described in almost loving terms in a since-declassified report written at Bletchley Park in 1945:It is regretted that it is not possible to give an adequate idea of the fascination of a Colossus at work: its sheer bulk and apparent complexity; the fantastic speed of thin paper tape round the glittering pulleys; the childish pleasure of not-not, span, print main heading and other gadgets; the wizardry of purely mechanical decoding letter by letter (one novice thought she was being hoaxed); the uncanny action of the typewriter in printing the correct scores without and beyond human aid; the stepping of display; periods of eager expectation culminating in the sudden appearance of the longed-for score; and the strange rhythms characterizing every type of run: the stately break-in, the erratic short run, the regularity of wheel-breaking, the stolid rectangle interrupted by the wild leaps of the carriage-return, the frantic chatter of a motor run, even the ludicrous frenzy of hosts of bogus scores.The demand for more ColossiBletchley Park’s managers, no longer leery of Flowers’s ideas, soon wanted additional Colossi. He finished building the second one in June 1944, days before D-Day and the Allied invasion of Europe. With 2,400 vacuum tubes—around 800 more than in Colossus I—Colossus II processed Tunny messages at an eye-watering speed of 25,000 characters per second.Its maximized timing-pulse rate was not far short of the performance of the first Intel microprocessor chip from the 1970s, more than 30 years later.Flowers conceded that “Colossus bore about as much resemblance to a modern computer as Stephenson’s [1829] Rocket locomotive did to the Royal Scot,” a state-of-the-art 20th-century train operating between London and Glasgow. But he emphasized that, nevertheless, Colossus “embodied all the basic features of a modern computer.” In Colossus, Flowers had pioneered clock pulses, bit-stream generators, control circuits, loops, counters, shift registers, interrupts, parallel processing, and more.As the Allies slowly fought their way toward Germany, the Colossi poured out wheel information, and the codebreakers provided the military with an unparalleled view of German strategies, strengths, weaknesses, and tactical intentions.Even with that mass of detailed intelligence, it took the Allies almost a year to move from Northern France to the German heartland. No one can say for sure how much longer the fighting would have lasted if the intelligence breakthrough had not occurred. But if Colossus and the codebreakers shortened the war even by only six months, the number of lives saved was in the millions.There were 10 Colossi at Bletchley Park by the end of the war, housed in two vast, steel-frame, bombproof buildings, running day and night. Although concealed behind a thick veil of secrecy, Bletchley Park accommodated the world’s first electronic computing facility. It was directed by Max Newman, the mathematician who mentored Turing in prewar Cambridge.I don’t think they understood very clearly what I was proposing until they actually had the machine. They just couldn’t believe it!”—Tommy FlowersWhen the fighting ended, authorities decided that ultrasecrecy must be maintained, and orders were issued to break up the Colossi. Only two were spared.“All that was left were the deep holes in the floor where the machines had stood,” Colossus operator Dorothy Du Boisson recalled in an interview for the book Colossus: The Secrets of Bletchley Park’s Codebreaking Computers. Norman Thurlow, one of Flowers’s engineers who was also interviewed, remembered being told in a staff memo that if the secrecy was ever lifted, he and his colleagues might be able to tell their grandchildren about Colossus and “the tapes that span on silver wheels.”IEEE Milestone dedication at Bletchley ParkThe Milestone plaque recognizing Colossus is to be displayed outside Block H at Bletchley Park, near Milton Keynes, England.The plaque is to read:Six Colossus codebreaking computers operated in this building in 1944–1945. Designed by Thomas H. Flowers of the British Post Office, they enabled deciphering of encrypted radio messages transmitted between German commands across occupied Europe, North Africa, and the Soviet Union. The resulting military intelligence saved countless lives and helped shorten World War II. As the first successful large-scale application of digital electronics to computing, Colossus anticipated subsequent computer developments.The IEEE United Kingdom and Ireland Section sponsored the nomination.Reviewed by the IEEE History Committee and awarded by the IEEE Board of Directors, IEEE Milestones recognize outstanding technical developments around the world that are at least 25 years old. The Milestone program is administered by the IEEE history and heritage group.To learn more about historical figures in engineering, IEEE Milestones, and IEEE History Center programs and events, check out our IEEE Tech History collection. Entertainment.title: Aston Martin Builds Just 50 Units of the Vanquish 25 to Mark 25 Years of the Iconic GT
Entertainment.text: SummaryEach example features an exclusive Q Skye Silver paint finish complemented by metal foil detailing on the side sills and shield vanes along with unique 21-inch forged alloy wheels featuring a subtle "V" motifThe interior is upgraded with laser-etched trim inlays, "Vanquish 25" embroidery on the seatbacks and a red center-accented start-stop rotary button inspired by the original 2001 modelThe vehicle retains the third-generation Vanquish’s 5.2-liter twin-turbo V12 engine delivering 823 hp and 738 lb-ft of torque to achieve a 214 mph top speedAston Martin has introduced the Vanquish 25 to celebrate a quarter-century since the iconic V12 grand tourer first appeared. Dubbed the Vanquish 25, the commemorative release pays homage to the original 2001 flagship designed by Ian Callum. The bespoke Q by Aston Martin commissioning service handled the entire creation process, capping the new model at an incredibly strict 50 units globally. Production is split perfectly down the middle, yielding 25 Coupe and 25 Volante examples. Rather than engineering a stripped-out track weapon, the manufacturer opted for a masterclass in subtle elegance and refined heritage.The exterior styling presents a sophisticated nod to the early millennium flagship. Every single car leaves the factory coated in an exclusive Q Skye Silver paint finish. Metal foil detailing traces the side sills and shield vanes to add a distinct layer of visual depth. Unique stainless steel side strakes and a custom Q Commission exhaust finisher further elevate the rear profile. A set of exclusive 21-inch forged alloy wheels manages the stance while featuring a subtle diamond-turned V motif that anchors the anniversary theme.Inside the cabin, the bespoke treatment continues with an emphasis on heritage craftsmanship. The interior pairs premium Semi-Aniline leather with soft Alcantara upholstery arranged in a diamond quilting pattern that directly references the 2001 original. Laser-etched trim inlays blend past and present styling cues flawlessly. At the center of the console sits a specially commissioned rotary start-stop button finished in satin silver with a vibrant red center. Buyers can configure the space in three distinct colorways including Onyx Black, Oxford Tan or Phantom Grey while subtle embroidery on the seats reminds occupants of the vehicle's rarity.Performance remains utterly staggering beneath the hood. Without any artificial restrictions, the celebratory model retains the modern 5.2-liter twin-turbo V12 engine. Engineers ensured the updated powertrain delivers a massive 823 horsepower and 738 lb-ft of torque straight to the rear wheels. This allows the heavy grand tourer to sprint from zero to 62 mph in a blistering 3.3 seconds before topping out at 214 mph. Aston Martin slated the Vanquish 25 for its formal public unveiling at Monterey Car Week in California this August. First deliveries are projected to reach highly vetted clients by the fourth quarter of the year.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: JJJJound x PORTER Engineer a Four-Piece Black Bag Capsule Around Pure Function
Entertainment.text: SummaryJJJJound and PORTER have built a four-piece bag collection spanning a key pack, drawstring bag, messenger bag and backpackEach piece shares a Teflon-coated nylon ripstop build with a quilted jacquard lining and JJJJound-branded metal hardwareThe capsule leans on function-first detailing designed for commuting, cycling and everyday city useJJJJound and PORTER have joined forces on a four-piece bag collection that puts technical function ahead of everything else. The Montreal design studio and the Japanese bag house built the capsule around silhouettes suited to daily situations like commuting and cycling, uniting a key pack, a drawstring bag, a messenger bag and a backpack under a single all-black, purpose-driven design language.The material runs consistently across all four carries. Each piece uses an outer of nylon ripstop treated with a water-repellent finish, giving the collection tear strength and enough protection to handle light rain, paired with tarpaulin for structure. Inside, the lining is a quilted nylon jacquard with the PORTER logo delicately woven throughout. Hardware ties the set together too, with high-quality metal name tags, buckles and cord stoppers all carrying the JJJJound logo, while the three larger bags add an original Tyvek name tag inside.The Key Pack is the most compact entry, a small holder for coins and cards that weighs just 120 grams. It arrives with a detachable neck strap, so it can hang as a lanyard or convert into a standalone pouch, and the interior includes a double ring for organizing keys. Stepping up in size, the Drawstring Bag works as a grab-and-go carry for a wallet or smartphone. Its side zippers open into pockets for quick-access items, and the shoulder straps use joints plus a wide length-adjustment range, making the bag easy to shed when wearing bulky outerwear or to switch between hand, shoulder and cross-body carry.The two largest pieces bring the most utility. The Messenger Bag is sized for everyday city movement, fitting A4 documents inside. Its flap adds a zippered pocket for a phone and integrates a PALS "Pouch Attachment Ladder System," letting wearers mount pouches and accessories along evenly spaced nylon webbing, while a reflective stretch cord secures a shirt or light layer on the outside. The Backpack rounds out the group as a 19-liter daypack. It keeps things organized with a flat interior pocket inside the front compartment and carries the same reflective stretch cord system for lashing down extra layers on the move.The JJJJound x PORTER collection drops July 24 at PORTER retail locations across Asia and via the Yoshida & Co. official online store.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Sacha Baron Cohen Resurrects Ali G for ‘Who Iz I?,’ His Secret Directorial Debut Landing in October
Entertainment.text: SummarySacha Baron Cohen has revealed a secret Ali G movie titled 'Ali G: Who Iz I?' through Amazon MGM StudiosThe film marks Cohen's feature directorial debut and reaches theaters on October 23Cohen shot the project covertly, mirroring the guerrilla approach behind his 'Borat' filmsSacha Baron Cohen has officially unveiled Ali G: Who Iz I?, a secret movie built around his fictional Londoner that arrives in theaters on October 23 through Amazon MGM Studios. The project doubles as a milestone for the comedian, marking his feature directorial debut after decades of playing provocateurs in front of the camera rather than behind it.True to form, Cohen broke the news without breaking character. He posted a video to Instagram fully as Ali G, framing the film as a long-overdue documentary about himself and leaning into the exaggerated London rude boy slang that made the character a phenomenon. The reveal fits a familiar Cohen playbook, since he filmed the movie in secret, the same guerrilla method he used for Borat in 2006 and its 2020 sequel. Working undercover, Cohen tends to interview real people who have no idea they are talking to a character, a setup that has historically produced both comedy and genuine discomfort.The return carries real history behind it. Cohen originated Ali G for Channel 4's The 11 O'Clock Show in 1998, then gave the character his own platform with Da Ali G Show in the early 2000s. He carried the fictional Londoner to the big screen once before in the 2002 film Ali G Indahouse, directed by Mark Mylod, cementing the character as a fixture of late-'90s and early-2000s British comedy well before Borat entered the picture. Across those years, Ali G built his reputation by ambushing high-profile figures, sitting down with the likes of Noam Chomsky, Andy Rooney and Newt Gingrich, all of whom were left bewildered by the fake interviewer across the table.Ali G: Who Iz I? arrives in theaters on October 23 via Amazon MGM Studios. Entertainment.title: LEGO Rebuilds the 1981 ‘Donkey Kong’ Arcade Cabinet as a Working Brick Homage
Entertainment.text: SummaryLEGO Super Mario is releasing a 'Donkey Kong' arcade set that recreates the classic arcade game in brick formThe build features Jumpman, Donkey Kong and Lady across a playable scaffold level with working barrel mechanicsThe 18+ collectible is positioned as retro decor for adult fans of video game historyLEGO Super Mario is turning one of gaming's foundational moments into a display piece with the Donkey Kong Arcade, a brick-built tribute to the original arcade cabinet. The 18+ set recreates the barrel-launching, ladder-climbing action of the classic game, pairing authentic play features with a form built to sit on a shelf as nostalgic decor rather than a toy.The set leans hard into the source material that started it all. Donkey Kong first hit arcades in 1981 as Nintendo's breakout hit, and it introduced two characters who would go on to define the company: the barrel-hurling ape himself and a mustachioed carpenter originally called Jumpman, who was soon renamed Mario and became the face of the entire industry. LEGO nods directly to that origin by naming the minifigure Jumpman rather than Mario, alongside Donkey Kong and Lady, staying faithful to the era the cabinet came from.That authenticity carries into how the model plays. Rather than a static diorama, the build recreates a Donkey Kong arcade level with scaffold, ladder and hammer details, plus a mechanism that circulates the barrels in a continuous loop. Builders pull a lever to release one of 21 barrels at a time, as if hurled by Donkey Kong, then steer Jumpman with a joystick and hit a button to make him leap over the obstacles. The interactivity mirrors the tension of the original game, where timing each jump was the whole challenge, and translates it into a physical, hands-on experience.Under the nostalgia sits a substantial build. The set comprises roughly 1,367 pieces and comes together into a finished model that stands over 15.5 inches (39 centimeters) high, 10.5 inches (27 centimeters) wide and 5.5 inches (15 centimeters) deep, giving it a footprint sized to anchor a shelf or desk rather than disappear into one. The vertical, cabinet-inspired proportions echo the upright arcade machine it references, letting the scaffold-and-ladder level climb the way the original screen did.Every element reinforces the collectible framing. The scaffold, ladder and hammer details recreate a full Donkey Kong stage rather than a single snapshot, while the looping barrel mechanism keeps the display in motion instead of frozen. Marked for ages 18 and up, the model is positioned as retro decor for a game room, shelf or home office, and slots into LEGO's wider assortment of sets for adults built around mindful, hands-on assembly, doubling as both a gamer gift and a piece of video game memorabilia.The LEGO Super Mario Donkey Kong Arcade is available to pre-order now via the official LEGO Shop, with orders shipping from August 1.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Xbox Brings Classic Original Games to PC for the First Time With New Backward Compatibility Program
Entertainment.text: Xbox has launched Xbox Backward Compatibility on PC, making a batch of classic original Xbox games playable on PC and handhelds for the first time. Rolling out today in early release, the program arrives with four legacy titles and support for devices including the ROG Xbox Ally and Xbox Ally X, marking the start of a broader push to preserve older Xbox games and carry them onto PC over time.The launch lineup pulls together four cult favorites from the original Xbox era. Players can jump into BLiNX: The Time Sweeper, Conker: Live and Reloaded, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge and Fuzion Frenzy starting today in supported regions. All four are now available to purchase on PC and come included with every Xbox Game Pass plan, giving both new players and returning fans multiple ways in.Ownership carries across hardware, too. Anyone who already holds a digital license for these games on console will see it transfer to PC and handheld automatically. Through Xbox Play Anywhere and Xbox Cloud Gaming, that means the same title can move between console, cloud, PC and handheld without a second purchase, reinforcing the cross-device flexibility at the center of the program.Beyond simply making the games playable, Xbox has layered in enhancements that preserve the original gameplay while sharpening it for modern hardware. The titles support customizable graphics settings, including up to 4x resolution upscaling, VSync, fullscreen and windowed display modes, anisotropic filtering and enhanced anti-aliasing, alongside customizable language and audio options. More is on the way as well, with Achievements set to arrive for the first four games in the coming months as one of the most requested additions. Access runs through the Xbox on PC app for any system that meets the minimum requirements, which start at Windows 11, 8 GB of RAM, and a GPU on the level of an Nvidia GTX 950 or AMD Radeon RX 550.Xbox Backward Compatibility on PC is available now in early release, with all four launch titles playable through the Xbox on PC app and included across Xbox Game Pass plans.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

One such marker is phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217), a modified variant of the tau protein involved in Alzheimer's disease pathology. People with higher levels in a blood sample have a greater chance of developing Alzheimer's disease symptoms in the years ahead, as the mechanisms of neurodegeneration are already operating at a higher than average level in their brain cells. Tau becomes pathological and damaging when it is hyperphosphorylated, aggregating and provoking chronic inflammation in brain tissue.
